newsitem.title: UK: Weighing up the costs of Labour's windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: Weighing up the costs of Labour's windfall tax.

text.p: British utilities are braced for a one-off "windfall" tax from an incoming Labour government but they are unsure just which of them will have to pay or how much.

"There is a dearth of detail...the major uncertainties are the overall size of the tax, who will pay, legality (and) the basis of allocation," analysts at Union Banque of Switzerland (UBS) said in a recent report.

Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown, likely to be named on Friday as Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, has said the windfall tax would "comfortably finance" a three billion pound ($4.9 billion) plan to help the young and long-term unemployed back into work.

This has led most analysts to believe that the windfall tax, which will be a major plank of Brown's first budget, could be up to five billion pounds, although figures as high as 10 billion have been suggested.
Brown said on Friday a budget would be held within two months to implement the windfall tax.
A possible windfall tax of five billion pounds appears to have been factored in to share prices, analysts say.
"The sector would react badly if the levy is significantly above five billion pounds," said Nigel Hawkins, analyst at Yamaichi.
Labour refuses to be drawn on specific targets for the tax but has referred to privatised firms which have made "excess profits" and are regulated by statute.
That could cast a net wide enough to include water and electricity companies, British Telecom, the former British Gas utility Centrica and even Railtrack and British Airports Authority.

But Labour has reserved its fiercest criticism for water companies, condemning them for hefty dividends and fat executive pay packets, while it claims more than 800 million gallons a day of supplies leak out of pipes as Britons face a hosepipe ban heading into the summer.

Brown said earlier this week that the British people would be "outraged" at the expected profits of the companies and would "regard a government that failed to deal with this problem as a government that had failed."
The privatised water and electricity companies report annual results in May and June.

Labour "could make the catchment base very broad to minimise legal problems but then set the actual parameters to weigh it towards water and electricity," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
Analysts believe that Labour will have to keep the net for the tax very wide in order to avoid being accused of discrimination.
Labour has said that it is "100 percent convinced that there will be no legal, financial or technical obstacles" to the planned levy.
Assuming a five billion pound overall levy, it is still unclear what criteria would be used to fix the amount payable by each company.
Analysts have focused on two ways the levy could be split among the companies involved -- premiums to flotation price and total returns to shareholders versus an industry average.
"To encompass charges that the assets were sold 'too cheaply'...one approach is to examine total returns to shareholders relative to an aggregate index," Goldman Sachs said in a recent report.

"It seems likely that a measure would be adopted which takes account both of the initial value of the companies on flotation and the excess returns since then," the Institute of Fiscal Studies said in a report in April.
A further variable in calculations by analysts is the timescale which Labour might adopt for assessing such "excess profits."

There seems a general consensus that in the case of the regional electricity companies (Recs), a cut-off point should come before the start of a flood of bids which racked up share prices and swept all but one of the original 12 Recs into a predator's hands.

Seven of the Recs are now owned by U.S. companies and some observers suggested that it might prove difficult to separate out their tax liability and could be politically sensitive ahead of Anglo-U.S. talks on business mergers.
But U.S.-based CalEnergy has already said it has established a liability for the tax likely on Northern Electric, which it bought last year.
"Whichever measure of excess profits is used, the results are very sensitive to the time period chosen," Goldman Sachs cautioned.

"Some companies perform very well over long periods of time but quite poorly recently...while others have turned in a more consistent performance," research group Oxera said in a report on the windfall tax published in its March edition of Utility Finance.

Goldman Sachs gives a range of 2.1-3.5 billion pounds in tax for electricity companies in its report, with 1.0-1.4 billion for water firms, up to 0.5 billion for gas while transport could be taxed between 0.2-0.6 billion and BT might face a levy of up to 0.4 billion.
But the report adds that "these seem broadly to be discounted in current share prices."
And analysts seem largely in agreement that the utilities will not suffer greatly through payment of a windfall tax.
"Even with a five billion windfall tax, the UK electricity and water utilities are able to offer attractive dividend growth," a report by Daiwa said in January. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
